subChunks.title: Tailwind Config Deep-Dive
subChunks.hookHtml: Most developers copy a tailwind.config.js from a starter and never open it again. That leaves half the framework on the table. The config is where a generic utility library becomes your design system — with your colours, your type scale, your spacing, and a theming strategy that survives a rebrand.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon's study is colder than the rest of the tower. Shelves hold scrolls sorted by intent, not by author. He sets down a quill and slides a parchment across the desk without looking up.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "The config is a constitution. Every token in your system either comes from it or ignores it at its peril. Sit. We begin with the single most expensive mistake a new wizard makes."

theme vs theme.extend — the critical difference

Using theme.colors replaces Tailwind's entire built-in palette. Using theme.extend.colors merges with it. Nine out of ten developers who "lost their grey-500" after touching the config made this mistake.

// ❌ WRONG — you just deleted the entire built-in palette
module.exports = {
  theme: {
    colors: {
      brand: '#6366f1',   // now bg-gray-100, bg-red-500, etc. are all gone
    }
  }
};

// ✅ CORRECT — extends without destroying
module.exports = {
  theme: {
    extend: {
      colors: {
        brand: { DEFAULT: '#6366f1', light: '#a5b4fc', dark: '#4338ca' },
        surface: '#f8fafc',
      }
    }
  }
};

Once you extend colours, Tailwind auto-generates bg-brand, text-brand, border-brand, bg-brand-light, text-brand-dark, and every other utility for free. You get the entire variant lattice for any multi-shade token.

Other common extensions

theme: {
  extend: {
    fontFamily: {
      display: ['Cal Sans', 'sans-serif'],
      mono: ['JetBrains Mono', 'monospace'],
    },
    spacing: {
      '18': '4.5rem',   // now p-18, m-18, w-18 all work
      '88': '22rem',
    },
    screens: {
      '3xl': '1920px',  // ultra-wide breakpoint
      'xs': '480px',    // small-phone breakpoint below sm
    },
    borderRadius: {
      '4xl': '2rem',
    },
    boxShadow: {
      'glow': '0 0 20px 4px rgb(99 102 241 / 0.4)',
    },
  }
}

The CSS-variable colour pattern — the RIGHT way to theme

This pattern is how every serious design system handles dark mode, white-labelling, and theming. It connects Tailwind utilities to CSS custom properties, giving you the best of both worlds.

// tailwind.config.js
theme: {
  extend: {
    colors: {
      // The <alpha-value> placeholder lets Tailwind wire in opacity modifiers
      // so bg-primary/50 (50% opacity) still works
      primary: 'rgb(var(--color-primary) / <alpha-value>)',
      'primary-foreground': 'rgb(var(--color-primary-foreground) / <alpha-value>)',
      background: 'rgb(var(--color-background) / <alpha-value>)',
      foreground:  'rgb(var(--color-foreground) / <alpha-value>)',
    }
  }
}

// index.css
:root {
  --color-primary:            99 102 241;   /* indigo-500 */
  --color-primary-foreground: 255 255 255;
  --color-background:         248 250 252;
  --color-foreground:         15 23 42;
}
.dark {
  --color-primary:            165 180 252;  /* indigo-300 */
  --color-background:         15 23 42;
  --color-foreground:         248 250 252;
}

// Usage in a component:
<button class="bg-primary text-primary-foreground hover:bg-primary/90">
  Save
</button>

Now flipping to dark mode is a single class toggle on <html>. Re-theming for a white-label client is editing four CSS variables. The Tailwind utilities don't change at all.

Plugins

// tailwind.config.js
plugins: [
  require('@tailwindcss/forms'),       // better default form styles
  require('@tailwindcss/typography'),  // .prose for rich text rendering
  // Custom plugin:
  function({ addUtilities }) {
    addUtilities({
      '.scrollbar-hide': {
        '-ms-overflow-style': 'none',
        'scrollbar-width': 'none',
        '&::-webkit-scrollbar': { 'display': 'none' },
      },
    });
  },
],

Custom plugins let you add one-off utilities that participate in JIT purging, just like built-in ones.

Fighting third-party specificity

// tailwind.config.js
// Wraps ALL generated utilities in #app { ... } so they beat
// any component library class without !important
important: '#app',

Solomon: "The config is not a file you set once and forget. It is the ledger where every design decision your system has committed to is recorded. Consult it before reaching for an arbitrary value."

storyBeats.text: The Grand Archmage's study is quiet except for the scratch of his quill. He does not look up when you enter — but a parchment slides across the desk toward you.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: Every junior wizard who 'lost their greys' after touching the config made the same mistake. theme.colors replaces the palette. theme.extend.colors adds to it. This is not subtle. This is the foundation.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: Connect your tokens to CSS variables. Then dark mode, white-labelling, and rebranding all become a matter of changing variable values — not hunting through thousands of class strings.

storyBeats.speaker: CSS-variable colour token
storyBeats.text: primary: 'rgb(var(--color-primary) / <alpha-value>)'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: A teammate uses theme.colors instead of theme.extend.colors to add a brand colour. The next day half the UI looks wrong. Explain exactly what happened, why it happened, and what the correct fix is.

questions.questionHtml: What is the difference between theme.colors and theme.extend.colors in tailwind.config.js?
options: theme.colors replaces the built-in palette entirely; theme.extend.colors merges with it
theme.colors only applies to text; theme.extend.colors applies to all properties
They are identical — just two ways to write the same thing
theme.colors is for primitives; theme.extend.colors is for semantic tokens only
questions.correctAnswer: theme.colors replaces the built-in palette entirely; theme.extend.colors merges with it
questions.explanationHtml: Using theme.colors wipes out Tailwind's built-in greys, reds, blues, and every other colour. Using theme.extend.colors adds your tokens on top of the defaults.

questions.questionHtml: What does the <alpha-value> placeholder in a CSS-variable colour token enable?
options: Tailwind's opacity modifier syntax, e.g. bg-primary/50
The dark: variant to auto-invert the colour
Automatic contrast checking for accessibility
Gradient generation for the colour
questions.correctAnswer: Tailwind's opacity modifier syntax, e.g. bg-primary/50
questions.explanationHtml: When you write 'rgb(var(--color-primary) / <alpha-value>)', Tailwind substitutes the opacity fraction at build time, enabling classes like bg-primary/50 or text-primary/75.

questions.questionHtml: You need a custom spacing value of 4.5rem that you'll use frequently. Where should you define it?
options: theme.extend.spacing in tailwind.config.js as '18': '4.5rem'
As an arbitrary value p-[4.5rem] wherever needed
In a global CSS variable and use it with @apply
As a CSS class with margin: 4.5rem in index.css
questions.correctAnswer: theme.extend.spacing in tailwind.config.js as '18': '4.5rem'
questions.explanationHtml: Extending the spacing scale makes p-18, m-18, w-18, gap-18, and all other spacing utilities available with the custom value. Arbitrary values are for genuine one-offs, not repeated values.

questions.questionHtml: Which config option helps Tailwind utilities win over third-party component library styles without adding !important to every class?
options: important: '#app'
prefix: 'tw-'
corePlugins: { all: true }
safelist: ['!important']
questions.correctAnswer: important: '#app'
questions.explanationHtml: important: '#app' wraps every generated utility rule in #app { ... }, giving them higher specificity than most component library classes without polluting your markup with !.

questions.questionHtml: A startup built their entire product using text-indigo-600 and bg-indigo-500 across 300 files. Marketing now wants the brand colour changed to teal. A developer says it's a "quick find-and-replace." A senior engineer disagrees. Who is right, and what should the codebase have done from the start?
questions.correctAnswer: The senior is right — find-and-replace of colour names is fragile and misses edge cases like indigo-500 used for non-brand purposes. The codebase should have defined theme.extend.colors.brand pointing to a CSS variable, then used bg-brand everywhere. Changing the brand is now one CSS variable update.
questions.explanationHtml: Find-and-replace conflates every use of indigo with brand intent. Some indigo uses may be decorative, not brand. A semantic token (bg-brand backed by a CSS variable) separates intent from palette, making a rebrand trivially safe.

subChunks.title: clsx, tailwind-merge, and CVA
subChunks.hookHtml: Knowing utility classes is the easy part. The hard part is wiring them to component logic — variants, props, overrides — without your JSX becoming an unreadable string of concatenated conditions. Three small libraries solve this completely, and every serious React + Tailwind codebase uses them.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sable the Illuminator has arranged three crystal vials on Solomon's workbench. Each is small, almost overlooked beside the Archmage's thick tomes. But Sable's eyes are sharp.

Sable the Illuminator: "These three — clsx, tailwind-merge, class-variance-authority — are the entire authoring layer for Tailwind in React. Master them and your components become readable. Ignore them and you will be maintaining spaghetti string concatenation forever."

Problem 1: Complex conditional classes

String concatenation works but becomes unreadable fast:

// Readable now, nightmare at 10 conditions
<button className={'px-4 py-2 rounded ' + (isPrimary ? 'bg-blue-600 text-white' : 'bg-gray-100 text-gray-700') + (isDisabled ? ' opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed' : '')}>

clsx is the solution. It accepts strings, objects, and arrays, filtering out falsy values:

import { clsx } from 'clsx';

// Strings
clsx('px-4 py-2', 'rounded')  // → 'px-4 py-2 rounded'

// Conditional expressions
clsx('px-4 py-2', isActive && 'bg-blue-600', isDisabled && 'opacity-50')
// → 'px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600'  (if active, not disabled)

// Object syntax (key = class, value = condition)
clsx('px-4 py-2', {
  'bg-blue-600 text-white': isPrimary,
  'bg-gray-100 text-gray-700': !isPrimary,
  'opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed': isDisabled,
})

// Arrays are flattened
clsx(['px-4 py-2', isActive && 'ring-2'])

Problem 2: Tailwind class conflicts when merging

Here is the subtle but critical problem. If a parent component sets px-4 and a caller passes className="px-8", both classes end up on the element. Which wins depends on which one appears later in Tailwind's generated stylesheet — and that order is not guaranteed to match your mental model.

// Component internals
<button className={clsx('px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600', className)}>

// Caller passes
<MyButton className="px-8" />

// Result: class="px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 px-8"
// Which px wins? Depends on stylesheet order. Unpredictable.

tailwind-merge understands Tailwind's utility groups and resolves conflicts intelligently — the last class in the group wins:

import { twMerge } from 'tailwind-merge';

twMerge('px-4 py-2', 'px-8')     // → 'py-2 px-8'
twMerge('text-sm', 'text-lg')    // → 'text-lg'
twMerge('bg-red-500', 'bg-blue-600')  // → 'bg-blue-600'

// It understands related groups too:
twMerge('p-4', 'px-8')           // → 'p-4 px-8'  (px-8 overrides only x-axis)

The cn() pattern — combine both

This is the universal pattern. You will find it in every serious codebase, usually in lib/utils.ts:

// lib/utils.ts
import { clsx, type ClassValue } from 'clsx';
import { twMerge } from 'tailwind-merge';

export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
  return twMerge(clsx(inputs));
}

// Usage in any component:
<button
  className={cn(
    'px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-md font-medium',  // base
    className,            // caller override — conflicts resolved by twMerge
    isDisabled && 'opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed',              // runtime condition
    isLoading && 'relative text-transparent',                   // another condition
  )}
>

class-variance-authority (CVA) — typed component variants

When a component has multiple variants (primary/secondary/ghost) and sizes (sm/md/lg), CVA gives you a typed, readable declaration instead of nested ternaries:

import { cva, type VariantProps } from 'class-variance-authority';

const button = cva(
  // Base classes applied to ALL variants
  'inline-flex items-center justify-center font-medium rounded-md transition-colors duration-150 focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-offset-2 disabled:opacity-50 disabled:pointer-events-none',
  {
    variants: {
      variant: {
        primary:     'bg-blue-600 text-white hover:bg-blue-700 focus-visible:ring-blue-500',
        secondary:   'bg-white text-gray-700 border border-gray-300 hover:bg-gray-50 focus-visible:ring-gray-400 shadow-sm',
        ghost:       'text-gray-700 hover:bg-gray-100 focus-visible:ring-gray-400',
        destructive: 'bg-red-600 text-white hover:bg-red-700 focus-visible:ring-red-500',
      },
      size: {
        sm: 'text-xs px-3 py-1.5 gap-1.5',
        md: 'text-sm px-4 py-2 gap-2',
        lg: 'text-base px-6 py-3 gap-2.5',
      },
    },
    defaultVariants: { variant: 'primary', size: 'md' },
  }
);

// TypeScript type for the variant props:
type ButtonProps = VariantProps<typeof button> & React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement> & {
  className?: string;
};

function Button({ variant, size, className, ...props }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button className={cn(button({ variant, size }), className)} {...props} />;
}

// Usage — fully typed, IntelliSense shows all options:
<Button variant="secondary" size="lg">Cancel</Button>
<Button variant="destructive">Delete account</Button>

Sable: "This is how Shadcn/ui builds every component. The variant declaration is the component's contract. It's not just a style choice — it's a typed API."

CVA shines in compound components too. An IconButton can compose the button variant, adding an icon variant on top without duplicating base classes.

storyBeats.text: Sable the Illuminator arranges three small crystal vials on the workbench. They look almost trivial — but every master's work you've seen lately has used all three.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: String concatenation works until it doesn't. clsx cleans up conditional logic. tailwind-merge resolves conflicts when classes collide. Compose them both into cn() and you never think about either problem again.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: cva goes further — it declares ALL your component variants in one typed block. This is how Shadcn/ui works. Once you understand this pattern you can read any modern component library.

storyBeats.speaker: The cn() utility
storyBeats.text: export function cn(...inputs) { return twMerge(clsx(inputs)); }

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Without tailwind-merge, what bug occurs when a reusable component accepts a className prop and internally sets padding? Show the bug with a concrete example, then show how twMerge fixes it.

questions.questionHtml: What does twMerge('px-4 py-2', 'px-8') return?
options: 'py-2 px-8'
'px-4 py-2 px-8'
'px-4 py-2'
'px-8 py-2 px-4'
questions.correctAnswer: 'py-2 px-8'
questions.explanationHtml: tailwind-merge understands that px-4 and px-8 are in the same utility group. The later value (px-8) wins and px-4 is dropped.

questions.questionHtml: What is the purpose of class-variance-authority (CVA)?
options: Declaring component variants in a typed, structured way that generates the correct class strings
Automatically resolving conflicting Tailwind utilities
Generating CSS variables from your config
Purging unused classes from the build output
questions.correctAnswer: Declaring component variants in a typed, structured way that generates the correct class strings
questions.explanationHtml: CVA takes a base class string and a variants object, returns a function that maps variant props to final class strings, and exposes TypeScript types for those props via VariantProps.

questions.questionHtml: A component applies className={cn('text-sm font-medium', props.className)}. A caller passes className="text-lg font-bold". What is the final resolved class string?
options: 'font-bold text-lg'
'text-sm font-medium text-lg font-bold'
'text-sm font-medium'
'text-lg font-medium'
questions.correctAnswer: 'font-bold text-lg'
questions.explanationHtml: tailwind-merge (via cn) resolves both text-sm/text-lg and font-medium/font-bold conflicts. The caller's classes win, producing font-bold text-lg.

questions.questionHtml: Which syntax is correct for using clsx to conditionally add a class?
options: clsx('base', isActive && 'bg-blue-600')
clsx('base', isActive ? true : 'bg-blue-600')
clsx('base' + isActive + 'bg-blue-600')
clsx('base', [isActive, 'bg-blue-600'])
questions.correctAnswer: clsx('base', isActive && 'bg-blue-600')
questions.explanationHtml: clsx filters out falsy values. When isActive is false, false && 'bg-blue-600' evaluates to false, which clsx ignores. When true, it evaluates to 'bg-blue-600', which clsx includes.

questions.questionHtml: A team reviews a PR. A junior built a button component with 12 variants using nested ternaries: variant === 'primary' ? 'bg-blue-600 ...' : variant === 'secondary' ? 'bg-white ...' : .... A senior asks them to rewrite it. What tool should they use, and what specific advantage does it give over ternaries besides readability?
questions.correctAnswer: CVA (class-variance-authority). Beyond readability, CVA exposes TypeScript types via VariantProps automatically, so callers get IntelliSense for valid variant values and TypeScript errors on invalid ones. The ternary approach has no types.
questions.explanationHtml: Nested ternaries are not typed — TypeScript cannot infer which strings are valid variant values. CVA's VariantProps<typeof buttonVariants> gives the component a proper typed API, catches typos at compile time, and documents the variant contract in one place.

subChunks.title: Accessibility with Tailwind
subChunks.hookHtml: Accessibility is not optional — it is a legal requirement under WCAG, the ADA, and the European Accessibility Act, and it is a professional expectation at every serious company. Tailwind gives you all the tools. Using them correctly is the mark of an expert.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Lyra the Scribe leads you down a spiral staircase to a room lit by a single lamp. A blindfolded figure sits at the desk, tracing a page with her fingertips. Lyra speaks quietly.

Lyra the Scribe: "A spell that works only for some readers is a spell half-cast. Let me show you the five habits that cover ninety percent of accessibility work in a Tailwind codebase."

Habit 1: focus-visible: over focus:

This is the single most common accessibility mistake in Tailwind projects.

// ❌ WRONG — shows a ring on every mouse click (annoying)
<button class="focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500">Save</button>

// ✅ CORRECT — ring appears only when focused via keyboard
<button class="focus:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500 focus-visible:ring-offset-2">Save</button>

focus-visible: maps to :focus-visible — a CSS pseudo-class the browser only applies when it believes focus came from the keyboard, not a mouse click. This is what designers mean when they say "remove the focus outline" — they mean for mouse users. Keyboard users still need it, and removing it entirely is a WCAG violation.

Habit 2: sr-only for icon-only controls

Every icon-only button must have a text label for screen readers:

<button class="p-2 rounded-md focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" class="w-5 h-5" />
  <span class="sr-only">Close dialog</span>
</button>

<!-- sr-only equivalent CSS (what Tailwind generates): -->
.sr-only {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px; height: 1px;
  padding: 0; margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip: rect(0,0,0,0);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border-width: 0;
}

The text is invisible on screen but announced by screen readers. Always mark SVG icons with aria-hidden="true" to prevent them being read aloud as noise.

Habit 3: ARIA state variants (Tailwind v3.2+)

Style from accessible state rather than toggling classes with JavaScript:

<!-- Chevron that rotates when dropdown opens -->
<button aria-expanded="false" class="flex items-center gap-2">
  Menu
  <svg class="w-4 h-4 transition-transform aria-expanded:rotate-180" />
</button>

<!-- Tab that shows active state -->
<button role="tab" aria-selected="false"
  class="px-4 py-2 text-sm border-b-2 border-transparent
         aria-selected:border-blue-600 aria-selected:text-blue-600 aria-selected:font-medium">
  Overview
</button>

<!-- Disabled state via aria -->
<button aria-disabled="true"
  class="px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 text-white aria-disabled:opacity-50 aria-disabled:cursor-not-allowed">
  Submit
</button>

This pattern keeps your ARIA attributes as the single source of truth for state. JS toggles the ARIA attribute; CSS responds to it. Cleaner than parallel class-and-attribute management.

Habit 4: Colour contrast

WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal body text and 3:1 for large text (18px+ or 14px+ bold). Several popular combinations fail:

// Contrast ratios against white background:
gray-400:   3.5:1  ❌ fails for body text
gray-500:   4.6:1  ✓ barely passes — prefer gray-600
gray-600:   5.9:1  ✓ solid
gray-700:   8.6:1  ✓ strong
slate-500:  4.6:1  ✓ barely — prefer slate-600 (6.9:1)
blue-400:   2.5:1  ❌ use blue-700 (5.5:1) for text on white

Use browser DevTools accessibility panel or webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/ before shipping any custom colour pairing.

Habit 5: Reduced motion

<div class="animate-bounce motion-reduce:animate-none">
<div class="transition-transform duration-300 motion-reduce:transition-none">

Users with vestibular disorders can be physically harmed by excessive motion. motion-reduce: maps to prefers-reduced-motion: reduce. Add it to every animated element — it costs nothing and can mean a great deal to someone.

Lyra: "Five habits. Write them on the wall above your desk. Every component you ship should pass all five before it leaves your branch."

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior developer why removing outline: none from a button is a WCAG violation, but using focus:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 is acceptable. What is the practical difference?

questions.questionHtml: What does sr-only do?
options: Visually hides content while keeping it accessible to screen readers
Removes content from the DOM and the accessibility tree
Hides content from screen readers but keeps it visually visible
Sets display: none on the element
questions.correctAnswer: Visually hides content while keeping it accessible to screen readers
questions.explanationHtml: sr-only uses position, size, clipping, and overflow CSS to make an element invisible on screen while keeping it in the accessibility tree, where screen readers can still announce it.

questions.questionHtml: What is the WCAG AA minimum contrast ratio for normal body text?
questions.explanationHtml: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18px+ or 14px+ bold). WCAG AAA raises these to 7:1 and 4.5:1 respectively.

questions.questionHtml: A dropdown button toggles aria-expanded between true and false in JavaScript. Which Tailwind approach correctly rotates a chevron icon when the dropdown is open?
options: class="transition-transform aria-expanded:rotate-180" on the chevron SVG
class="rotate-180" toggled by JavaScript alongside aria-expanded
class="open:rotate-180" which fires on the open state
class="expanded:rotate-180" which maps to aria-expanded
questions.correctAnswer: class="transition-transform aria-expanded:rotate-180" on the chevron SVG
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's aria-expanded: variant applies when the element (or its closest ARIA-attributable ancestor) has aria-expanded="true". This keeps JS responsible for ARIA, and CSS responds declaratively.

questions.questionHtml: Which is the correct way to add a keyboard focus ring to a button without showing it on mouse clicks?
options: focus:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500
focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500
outline-none hover:ring-2
focus:ring-0 active:ring-2
questions.correctAnswer: focus:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500
questions.explanationHtml: focus:outline-none removes the browser default outline for all focus events. focus-visible:ring-2 adds a ring only when the browser classifies the focus as keyboard-originated.

questions.questionHtml: An accessibility audit flags your icon-only notification bell button with: "Interactive element has no accessible name." The button contains only an SVG bell icon. What is the fix, and why is aria-label on the button alone not enough in Tailwind-idiomatic code?
questions.correctAnswer: Add Notifications inside the button AND mark the SVG with aria-hidden='true'. aria-label alone works but is less maintainable — the sr-only span keeps the label in the component's HTML where it is visible to code reviewers and translatable by i18n tools.
questions.explanationHtml: Both approaches pass WCAG. The sr-only pattern is preferred in React codebases because the label text is in the JSX where it's reviewable, translatable, and won't silently drift out of sync with the visual design. aria-label strings are invisible in rendered output and easy to forget to update.

subChunks.title: Performance and the JIT Scanner
subChunks.hookHtml: Tailwind v3's JIT compiler is the reason production CSS stays tiny. It only emits the classes you actually use. But it learns what you use by scanning your source files as plain text — not by executing your code. That distinction produces the #1 production bug in every Tailwind codebase.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Master Ember pulls a thin, well-thumbed volume from the shelf: The Scanner. He sets it on the workbench without opening it.

Master Ember: "Tailwind's great virtue is that it emits nothing you do not use. Its great trap is that it decides what you use by reading your source files as text — not executing them. If the scanner cannot see a complete class name as a string, that class does not exist in production."

How JIT works

At build time, Tailwind reads every file matching your content globs, looks for strings that match its utility patterns, and emits only those utilities. It does this with text matching — no JavaScript execution, no static analysis.

// tailwind.config.js
content: [
  './index.html',
  './src/**/*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}',
  // ✅ Include third-party component libraries that use Tailwind:
  './node_modules/@your-org/design-system/dist/**/*.js',
  // ❌ Do NOT include your own CSS output — circular scanning:
  // './dist/**/*.css'
],

The dynamic class trap — the #1 production bug

This is the most common Tailwind bug and it always manifests the same way: works in development, wrong in production.

// ❌ BROKEN — Tailwind scans these files and never sees
// 'text-red-500' or 'text-green-500' as complete strings.
// Only 'text-' + color + '-500' is in the source.
const statusClass = `text-${status === 'error' ? 'red' : 'green'}-500`;
<p className={statusClass}>{message}</p>

// In dev: the dev server may still have these from a previous build.
// In production: JIT purges them. The text has no colour.

// ✅ CORRECT — complete class strings appear in source
const statusClasses = {
  error:   'text-red-500',
  success: 'text-green-500',
  warning: 'text-yellow-500',
  info:    'text-blue-500',
};
<p className={statusClasses[status] ?? 'text-gray-500'}>{message}</p>

The rule is absolute: never construct a Tailwind class by interpolating a fragment of it. The full class string must appear verbatim somewhere in a file the scanner reads.

Safelisting — for genuinely dynamic classes

When class names come from a database, CMS, or external API, you cannot guarantee full strings in source. Use safelist:

// tailwind.config.js
safelist: [
  // Exact classes you know you need:
  'text-red-500',
  'text-green-500',
  // Pattern for a family of classes (useful for CMS colour choices):
  { pattern: /bg-(red|green|blue|yellow)-(100|500|900)/ },
  // With variants (the variants also need safelisting):
  { pattern: /bg-(red|green|blue)-(100|500)/, variants: ['hover', 'focus'] },
],

Use safelist sparingly — it bypasses purging and can bloat your bundle if the patterns are too broad.

Checking your bundle

After npm run build, inspect dist/assets/*.css. A well-configured production Tailwind build for a medium-sized app is typically 8–25 KB gzipped. Red flags:

  • 100+ KB: a content glob is probably matching node_modules or a large JSON file
  • Styles missing in production but present in dev: dynamic class interpolation bug
  • Styles present in dev but not needed: missing in safelist or content globs too broad

Arbitrary values — when they are and aren't appropriate

// ✅ Appropriate — one-off pixel-perfect value from design spec
<div class="top-[57px]">  // navbar is exactly 57px tall

// ❌ Not appropriate — value used in 15 places
<div class="mt-[17px]">   // extend spacing: { '4.25': '17px' } instead

// ✅ Appropriate — CSS calc or custom expressions
<div class="w-[calc(100%-theme(spacing.16))]">

Ember: "Arbitrary values are an escape hatch, not a shortcut. When you see them accumulating, the theme config is failing to represent the design system."

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to someone who only knows HTML/CSS why `text-${color}-500` works in development but breaks in production. Use the word 'scanner' in your explanation.

questions.questionHtml: How does Tailwind JIT determine which utility classes to include in the production build?
options: It scans source files listed in the content config as plain text, looking for complete class name strings
It executes your JavaScript code and tracks which classes are applied at runtime
It imports all possible utilities and tree-shakes unused ones at bundle time
It reads your CSS file and generates utilities for every selector found
questions.correctAnswer: It scans source files listed in the content config as plain text, looking for complete class name strings
questions.explanationHtml: JIT is a text scanner, not a JS evaluator. Complete class strings must be present verbatim in a scanned file. Interpolated fragments like `text-${color}-500` produce no complete class string and are therefore purged.

questions.questionHtml: When should you use safelist in tailwind.config.js?
options: When class names are determined by data from a CMS, database, or API at runtime
For all classes used in production to guarantee they are not purged
When you want faster build times by skipping the scanner
As an alternative to extending the theme config
questions.correctAnswer: When class names are determined by data from a CMS, database, or API at runtime
questions.explanationHtml: safelist bypasses the scanner for specific class patterns. It should be used sparingly — only for genuinely dynamic classes that cannot appear as complete strings in source.

questions.questionHtml: Which content glob configuration is WRONG?
options: './dist/**/*.css' — includes the compiled CSS output
'./src/**/*.{ts,tsx}' — includes TypeScript source files
'./index.html' — includes the HTML entry point
'./node_modules/@myorg/ui/dist/**/*.js' — includes a component library
questions.correctAnswer: './dist/**/*.css' — includes the compiled CSS output
questions.explanationHtml: Including your own compiled CSS output creates a circular scan — Tailwind generates CSS, scans it for class names, generates more CSS based on those names, etc. Always scan source files, never build output.

questions.questionHtml: A production build finishes and the CSS file is 180 KB gzipped. What is the most likely cause?
options: A content glob is too broad and is scanning node_modules or a large JSON data file
The safelist contains too few patterns
JIT is disabled and the legacy purge mode is running
The postcss config is missing a minification step
questions.correctAnswer: A content glob is too broad and is scanning node_modules or a large JSON data file
questions.explanationHtml: When the content globs accidentally cover files with thousands of random strings that match Tailwind utility patterns (like JSON data or the full node_modules), the scanner emits every matched utility. A typical app's CSS should be under 30 KB gzipped.

questions.questionHtml: A developer builds a status feed where post categories are fetched from an API. They write className={`bg-${post.category}-100 text-${post.category}-800`} and it works perfectly in development. QA signs it off. After deploying to production, all category badges show no background colour. Explain what happened and give two different valid fixes.
questions.correctAnswer: The JIT scanner saw template literals with interpolated fragments ('bg-' + category + '-100') but never a complete class string. In production those utilities were not emitted. Fix 1: a lookup object mapping each possible category to its complete class strings. Fix 2: add the specific class patterns to safelist with { pattern: /bg-(news|sport|tech)-(100|800)/ }.
questions.explanationHtml: The dev server often has a broader initial compilation, masking the bug. Production JIT is strict — only emit what the scanner found. The lookup-object approach is cleanest as it also handles future categories explicitly. Safelist is appropriate when the categories are truly unbounded or come from user input.

subChunks.title: Design Systems and Shadcn/ui
subChunks.hookHtml: Most production React + Tailwind apps don't build every component from scratch. Understanding how Shadcn/ui works — and why it's designed the way it is — teaches you the entire component-library architecture that underlies nearly every serious codebase you'll join in 2024 and beyond.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon closes the config scrolls and opens a slim codex with a dark cover. On the spine: Shadcn.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "Most students see a component library and ask: 'How do I install it?' The question that reveals mastery is: 'How is it built?' Because once you can read a Shadcn component, you can modify it, extend it, or replace it — and you'll never be held hostage by an upstream package again."

What Shadcn/ui is — and isn't

Shadcn/ui is not a traditional component library you install as a dependency. You run a CLI command and it copies component source code into your project. You own it entirely. This is intentional.

npx shadcn-ui@latest add button
# Creates: components/ui/button.tsx in YOUR project
# You can open it, read it, and change every class.

Architecture: Radix UI (accessible, unstyled primitives) + Tailwind CSS (styling) + CVA (variants) + cn() (merging).

Reading a Shadcn component

// components/ui/button.tsx (Shadcn-generated — now in YOUR project)
import { Slot } from '@radix-ui/react-slot';
import { cva, type VariantProps } from 'class-variance-authority';
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils';

const buttonVariants = cva(
  // Base: accessibility, transitions, disabled state all baked in
  'inline-flex items-center justify-center rounded-md text-sm font-medium ring-offset-background transition-colors focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-offset-2 disabled:pointer-events-none disabled:opacity-50',
  {
    variants: {
      variant: {
        default:     'bg-primary text-primary-foreground hover:bg-primary/90',
        destructive: 'bg-destructive text-destructive-foreground hover:bg-destructive/90',
        outline:     'border border-input bg-background hover:bg-accent hover:text-accent-foreground',
        secondary:   'bg-secondary text-secondary-foreground hover:bg-secondary/80',
        ghost:       'hover:bg-accent hover:text-accent-foreground',
        link:        'text-primary underline-offset-4 hover:underline',
      },
      size: {
        default: 'h-10 px-4 py-2',
        sm:      'h-9 rounded-md px-3',
        lg:      'h-11 rounded-md px-8',
        icon:    'h-10 w-10',
      },
    },
    defaultVariants: { variant: 'default', size: 'default' },
  }
);

interface ButtonProps
  extends React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>,
    VariantProps<typeof buttonVariants> {
  asChild?: boolean;
}

const Button = React.forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(
  ({ className, variant, size, asChild = false, ...props }, ref) => {
    const Comp = asChild ? Slot : 'button';
    return (
      <Comp
        className={cn(buttonVariants({ variant, size, className }))}
        ref={ref}
        {...props}
      />
    );
  }
);

Notice the CSS variables: bg-primary, text-primary-foreground, bg-destructive. These are not Tailwind built-ins — they are defined in globals.css:

/* globals.css — Shadcn theming layer */
:root {
  --background: 0 0% 100%;
  --foreground: 222.2 84% 4.9%;
  --primary: 222.2 47.4% 11.2%;
  --primary-foreground: 210 40% 98%;
  --secondary: 210 40% 96.1%;
  --secondary-foreground: 222.2 47.4% 11.2%;
  --destructive: 0 84.2% 60.2%;
  --destructive-foreground: 210 40% 98%;
  --ring: 222.2 84% 4.9%;
}

.dark {
  --background: 222.2 84% 4.9%;
  --foreground: 210 40% 98%;
  --primary: 210 40% 98%;
  --primary-foreground: 222.2 47.4% 11.2%;
}

/* tailwind.config.js wires them in: */
theme: {
  extend: {
    colors: {
      primary: { DEFAULT: 'hsl(var(--primary))', foreground: 'hsl(var(--primary-foreground))' },
    }
  }
}

When to use Shadcn vs build from scratch

  • Use Shadcn/Radix: Dialog, Select, Dropdown Menu, Toast, Command (search), Tooltip, Tabs, Accordion — anything with ARIA roles, focus management, or keyboard navigation. These are genuinely hard to implement correctly.
  • Build from scratch: Card, Badge, Divider, Skeleton, Avatar — simple visual components with no interactive behaviour. They don't need Radix; a few Tailwind classes is all they need.

The rule: if a component needs role, aria-* attributes, or keyboard event handling to be correct, use a primitive. Don't reinvent focus traps.

Solomon: "When you copy a Shadcn component into your project, you are not accepting a dependency — you are accepting responsibility. Read every line. Understand every class. Then it is yours."

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a colleague why Shadcn/ui copies source code into your project instead of being an installable npm package. What does that design decision enable that a traditional library cannot?

questions.questionHtml: How does Shadcn/ui differ from a traditional component library like Material UI?
options: Shadcn copies component source code into your project; you own and can modify every class
Shadcn is installed as an npm package and imported with tree-shaking
Shadcn generates components at runtime based on your theme config
Shadcn only works with Next.js and not standard React
questions.correctAnswer: Shadcn copies component source code into your project; you own and can modify every class
questions.explanationHtml: Running npx shadcn-ui add button writes components/ui/button.tsx into your repo. There is no runtime dependency. You can change any class, add any variant, or delete any behaviour. This is the entire design philosophy.

questions.questionHtml: What role does Radix UI play in the Shadcn/ui architecture?
options: Radix provides accessible, unstyled behaviour primitives (focus traps, ARIA, keyboard nav); Tailwind styles them
Radix provides a default visual theme that Shadcn overrides with Tailwind
Radix handles state management for interactive components
Radix is a CSS framework that Shadcn replaces with Tailwind utilities
questions.correctAnswer: Radix provides accessible, unstyled behaviour primitives (focus traps, ARIA, keyboard nav); Tailwind styles them
questions.explanationHtml: Radix focuses entirely on correct behaviour — keyboard navigation, focus management, ARIA attributes — without any visual opinion. Shadcn layers Tailwind classes on top. You get correctness for free and style completely.

questions.questionHtml: You need to customise a Shadcn Button so the primary variant uses your brand colour instead of the default dark theme. What do you change?
options: Update the --primary CSS variable in globals.css
Edit the npm package source in node_modules
Override the button's Tailwind classes with !important in your CSS
Pass a style prop with the colour directly to each Button usage
questions.correctAnswer: Update the --primary CSS variable in globals.css
questions.explanationHtml: Shadcn's theming is entirely driven by CSS variables defined in globals.css. Changing --primary to your brand's HSL values updates every component that uses bg-primary simultaneously, with no class changes needed.

questions.questionHtml: A team is building a custom dropdown menu. A junior suggests building it from scratch with Tailwind. A senior says to use Radix UI's DropdownMenu primitive and style it with Tailwind. The junior says they're the same amount of work. Who is right?
options: The senior — correct keyboard navigation, focus trapping, and ARIA for dropdowns requires significant effort; Radix handles all of it
The junior — a div with hover states is all a dropdown needs
Both are right — it depends on whether TypeScript is being used
The junior — Radix adds too much bundle weight for a simple dropdown
questions.correctAnswer: The senior — correct keyboard navigation, focus trapping, and ARIA for dropdowns requires significant effort; Radix handles all of it
questions.explanationHtml: An accessible dropdown needs: arrow key navigation, Escape to close, focus management on open/close, role="menu", aria-expanded, and more. This is non-trivial to implement correctly. Radix has done this work; use it.

questions.questionHtml: Six months after adding Shadcn to a project, a developer finds a bug in the Shadcn Dialog component — it doesn't correctly restore focus to the trigger element on close. They check the Shadcn GitHub and see it was fixed two weeks ago. How do they get the fix, and how does this differ from fixing a bug in Material UI?
questions.correctAnswer: Since Shadcn source lives in their project, they manually apply the fix — copy the relevant code change from the Shadcn GitHub diff into their components/ui/dialog.tsx. With Material UI (a package), they would run npm update. Shadcn's tradeoff: full control and no forced upgrades, but manual maintenance. Material UI's tradeoff: easy updates, but cannot modify internals.
questions.explanationHtml: This is the core Shadcn tradeoff. Owning the source means no version lock-in and full customisation, but it also means manually tracking upstream fixes. Teams should decide deliberately whether the trade is worth it for their project size and maintenance capacity.

subChunks.title: Portfolio-Ready Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: You know the utilities. You know the config, the tooling, the accessibility, the JIT scanner. Now assemble them into the patterns that appear on every portfolio and job-application project — the actual UI shapes that hiring managers and tech leads look at when evaluating your work.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Solomon leads you out of the library onto a balcony above the Academy courtyard. The Pattern Gardens stretch below — small, living examples of every common UI shape.

Grand Archmage Solomon: "Every product is a recombination of a handful of patterns. A hero section. A responsive nav. A card grid. A modal. A footer. Master these and you can scaffold any new screen in an afternoon."

Pattern 1: Responsive Navigation (fixed, glass morphism)

<nav class="fixed top-0 inset-x-0 z-50 bg-white/80 backdrop-blur-md border-b border-gray-100">
  <div class="container mx-auto px-4 h-16 flex items-center justify-between">
    <a href="/" class="text-xl font-bold text-gray-900 tracking-tight">Logo</a>

    <!-- Desktop nav links: hidden on mobile, flex on md+ -->
    <div class="hidden md:flex items-center gap-8">
      <a href="/about" class="text-sm text-gray-600 hover:text-gray-900 transition-colors">About</a>
      <a href="/work" class="text-sm text-gray-600 hover:text-gray-900 transition-colors">Work</a>
      <a href="/contact" class="text-sm font-medium px-4 py-1.5 bg-gray-900 text-white rounded-full hover:bg-gray-700 transition-colors">Contact</a>
    </div>

    <!-- Mobile menu button: visible on mobile, hidden on md+ -->
    <button class="md:hidden p-2 text-gray-600 hover:text-gray-900" aria-label="Open menu">
      <svg class="w-5 h-5" />
      <span class="sr-only">Open menu</span>
    </button>
  </div>
</nav>

<!-- Spacer so content clears the fixed nav -->
<div class="h-16"></div>

Pattern 2: Hero Section

<section class="min-h-screen flex items-center bg-gradient-to-br from-slate-900 to-slate-800 px-4">
  <div class="container mx-auto text-center">
    <span class="inline-flex items-center px-3 py-1 bg-blue-500/20 text-blue-400 rounded-full text-sm font-medium mb-6">
      Available for hire
    </span>
    <h1 class="text-5xl md:text-7xl font-bold text-white mb-6 tracking-tight">
      Full-Stack Developer
    </h1>
    <p class="text-xl text-slate-400 mb-10 max-w-2xl mx-auto leading-relaxed">
      Building performant, accessible web applications with React, TypeScript, and modern tooling.
    </p>
    <div class="flex gap-4 justify-center flex-wrap">
      <a href="/work"
         class="px-8 py-4 bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-500 text-white font-semibold rounded-lg transition-colors">
        View Work
      </a>
      <a href="/contact"
         class="px-8 py-4 bg-white/10 hover:bg-white/20 text-white font-semibold rounded-lg transition-colors border border-white/20">
        Get in Touch
      </a>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

Pattern 3: Project Card Grid with hover effects

<section class="py-24 bg-gray-50">
  <div class="container mx-auto px-4">
    <h2 class="text-3xl font-bold text-gray-900 mb-12 text-center">Selected Work</h2>
    <div class="grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-6">

      <!-- group enables group-hover: on children -->
      <article class="bg-white rounded-xl overflow-hidden shadow-sm hover:shadow-md transition-shadow group">
        <div class="aspect-video bg-gray-100 overflow-hidden">
          <img src="..." alt="Project screenshot"
               class="w-full h-full object-cover group-hover:scale-105 transition-transform duration-300" />
        </div>
        <div class="p-6">
          <div class="flex gap-2 mb-3">
            <span class="text-xs font-medium px-2 py-1 bg-blue-50 text-blue-700 rounded">React</span>
            <span class="text-xs font-medium px-2 py-1 bg-purple-50 text-purple-700 rounded">TypeScript</span>
          </div>
          <h3 class="text-lg font-semibold text-gray-900 mb-2">Project Name</h3>
          <p class="text-sm text-gray-600 leading-relaxed mb-4">A short description of the project.</p>
          <a href="/projects/x" class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-600 hover:text-blue-700 inline-flex items-center gap-1">
            View project
            <svg class="w-3 h-3" />
          </a>
        </div>
      </article>

    </div>
  </div>
</section>

Pattern 4: Footer

<footer class="bg-gray-900 text-gray-400 py-12">
  <div class="container mx-auto px-4 flex flex-col md:flex-row justify-between items-center gap-6">
    <div>
      <p class="text-white font-semibold mb-1">Your Name</p>
      <p class="text-sm">Full-Stack Developer — Available for contract work</p>
    </div>
    <div class="flex gap-6">
      <a href="https://github.com" class="text-sm hover:text-white transition-colors">GitHub</a>
      <a href="https://linkedin.com" class="text-sm hover:text-white transition-colors">LinkedIn</a>
      <a href="mailto:you@email.com" class="text-sm hover:text-white transition-colors">Email</a>
    </div>
  </div>
</footer>

How to approach a new portfolio project

  1. Start mobile-first. Design and code for the smallest breakpoint first. Breakpoint prefixes add to it.
  2. Establish a type hierarchy first. Decide your h1 (text-5xl), h2 (text-3xl), h3 (text-xl), body (text-base) before writing a single other class.
  3. Pick one accent colour and use three shades. light/100 for backgrounds, mid/600 for text, dark/900 for high-contrast. Avoid more than two accent colours.
  4. Use container mx-auto px-4 on every section wrapper. Never apply width constraints inside sections.
  5. Add transition-* to everything interactive from day one. Retrofitting animations is painful.
  6. Use group + group-hover: for card hover effects. This keeps hover logic on one element even when children need to respond.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the 'group + group-hover:' pattern for a project card that scales its image on hover. Why does this pattern work, and what alternative (and worse) approach might a junior developer reach for instead?

questions.questionHtml: Which combination of classes creates a full-viewport hero section that centers its content vertically and horizontally?
options: min-h-screen flex items-center justify-center
h-screen absolute top-1/2 left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2
vh-100 d-flex align-center justify-center
full-height flex-center
questions.correctAnswer: min-h-screen flex items-center justify-center
questions.explanationHtml: min-h-screen ensures the section is at least full viewport height. flex items-center justify-center centres the child both vertically and horizontally with flexbox.

questions.questionHtml: Which pair of classes creates a fixed navbar that has a frosted-glass effect over content below it?
options: fixed top-0 inset-x-0 bg-white/80 backdrop-blur-md
sticky top-0 bg-white opacity-80
absolute top-0 w-full blur-sm bg-white
fixed bg-white/80 filter blur
questions.correctAnswer: fixed top-0 inset-x-0 bg-white/80 backdrop-blur-md
questions.explanationHtml: fixed top-0 inset-x-0 pins the nav to the top of the viewport spanning full width. bg-white/80 makes it 80% opaque. backdrop-blur-md blurs the content visible through it — the frosted glass effect.

questions.questionHtml: You have a project card where hovering the card should scale the card image. Which pattern correctly applies the scale only to the image, triggered by hovering the card?
options: Add class 'group' to the card, then 'group-hover:scale-105 transition-transform' to the image
Add 'hover:scale-105' to both the card and the image
Add 'hover:*:scale-105' to the card to target all children
Use JavaScript to add 'scale-105' to the image on card mouseenter
questions.correctAnswer: Add class 'group' to the card, then 'group-hover:scale-105 transition-transform' to the image
questions.explanationHtml: The group class marks the parent. Any descendant with a group-hover: prefix applies that utility when the group ancestor is hovered. This keeps the hover trigger and the visual response cleanly separated without JavaScript.

questions.questionHtml: Which classes create an "available for hire" badge with a subtle translucent blue background — the kind seen on modern developer portfolios?
options: bg-blue-500/20 text-blue-400 rounded-full px-3 py-1 text-sm font-medium
bg-blue-100 text-blue-800 rounded px-2 py-1 text-xs
border-2 border-blue-500 text-blue-500 rounded-full px-3
bg-transparent outline outline-blue-400 text-blue-400 rounded-full
questions.correctAnswer: bg-blue-500/20 text-blue-400 rounded-full px-3 py-1 text-sm font-medium
questions.explanationHtml: The /20 opacity modifier on bg-blue-500 creates a 20% opaque blue background — the translucent effect. text-blue-400 is light enough to look good on a dark hero background. rounded-full produces the pill shape.

questions.questionHtml: A junior developer's portfolio hero section looks perfect on their 1440px laptop but the text is illegible on a 375px phone — the heading is 72px and overflows the screen. They ask what responsive prefix to add. What do you tell them, and what underlying principle did they miss when building it?
questions.correctAnswer: They should rewrite it mobile-first: start with text-4xl or text-3xl (legible on phone), then add md:text-5xl lg:text-7xl. The principle they missed: unprefixed utilities are the base (smallest screen). They built desktop-first and tried to 'fix' mobile with prefixes — but there is no max-width prefix to undo a large base size. Mobile-first means the base is the smallest. Larger screens add, never subtract.
questions.explanationHtml: There is no Tailwind equivalent of a 'max-sm:' prefix to decrease font size at small screens (it exists but is rarely idiomatic). The correct pattern is always to set the smallest-screen value as the base and override upward. Once this principle is internalised, responsive design becomes additive composition rather than defensive overriding.
